summary: Gives an overview of IPv4 and IPv6 deployment scenarios in light of the predicted depletion of IPv4 address blocks, noting that the transition has gone more slowly than expected. It is informational.

eli5.summary: The internet is running out of old-style addresses, like phone numbers. This note describes ways to live with both old and new numbers.

questions: what is ipv4 over ipv6 tunneling
subtitle: Deployment approaches for living with both IP versions as IPv4 addresses run out.

tldr.problem: IPv4 address space is running out faster than expected, and dual-stack deployment has been slower than anticipated, forcing networks to find ways to support both IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC identifies five key deployment scenarios and technical approaches, including carrier-grade NAT (CGN), IPv4-over-IPv6 tunneling, and IPv6-to-IPv4 translation, to handle the transition without requiring immediate abandonment of IPv4.
tldr.outcome: The document informed the rechartering of IETF working groups (Behave and Softwire) to develop standards for IPv4 and IPv6 co-existence, establishing the foundation for transition tools still in use today.

facts.label: Key enabling technology
facts.value: IPv4-over-IPv6 tunneling, Carrier-Grade NAT, NAT64 translation

today: RFC 6127 remains informational and has not been obsoleted. The Behave and Softwire working groups addressed its scenarios with multiple standards, including Dual-Stack Lite for IPv4-over-IPv6, NAT64 and DNS64 for translation, and various CGN specifications. While IPv6 deployment has continued to grow, these scenarios remain relevant as dual-stack and transitional deployments persist globally.

sections.title: The Transition Slower Than Expected
sections.content:
When IPv6 was designed, the shift from IPv4 to IPv6 was expected to happen quickly and smoothly. Instead, the IPv4 Internet grew much faster than anticipated, and IPv6 deployment has taken far longer than expected. Now, with IPv4 address pools predicted to deplete within years, network operators urgently need new approaches to handle a world where both IPv4 and IPv6 must coexist for a long time.

Rather than assuming a quick cutover to IPv6, current realities require looking beyond the traditional dual-stack approach (where each device runs both IPv4 and IPv6). The RFC outlines deployment models that were historically not the focus of standards work but are now essential for the industry to continue functioning as IPv4 becomes scarce.
sections.eli5: Experts thought everyone would switch to IPv6 quickly, but that hasn't happened. Now they need to figure out how to keep the internet working when there are not enough old-style addresses for everyone.

sections.title: Five Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC identifies five critical scenarios driving the need for new tools. First, reaching the IPv4 Internet with limited public addresses happens when service providers must share a single public IPv4 address among multiple subscribers. Second, running out of private address space affects very large service providers whose networks exhaust the RFC 1918 private address blocks reserved for internal use. Third, IPv6-only enterprise networks need to reach the public IPv4 Internet without dual-stack everywhere. Fourth, reaching IPv4-only servers from IPv6 clients allows enterprises to place aging servers on private addresses while still serving IPv6 users. Fifth, reaching IPv6-only servers from IPv4 clients prepares for a future where some servers move to IPv6-only.

Each scenario has different operational requirements and presents different engineering trade-offs between the number of devices that must change and the complexity of the solutions deployed.
sections.eli5: There are five main problems to solve: sharing addresses between subscribers, running out of internal addresses, having IPv6-only networks reach old servers, having new networks reach old servers, and having old networks reach brand new servers.

sections.title: Technical Approaches and Trade-Offs
sections.content:
For scenarios involving limited public address space, the RFC explores several approaches. NAT444 (double NAT) involves a Carrier-Grade NAT at the service provider layering on top of existing home gateways, but it breaks port-mapping and can cause operational complications. Distributed NAT splits address translation between the home gateway and the carrier network, dividing port ranges so the carrier can operate more statelessly. IPv4 over IPv6 tunneling allows carriers to build IPv6-only internal networks while still carrying IPv4 traffic in tunnels, and Dual-Stack Lite extends this to provide IPv4 service to subscribers even when they receive only IPv6 connectivity.

For IPv6-only networks reaching IPv4 servers, NAT64 and similar translation mechanisms map IPv6 addresses to private IPv4 addresses with corresponding DNS updates, though translation has inherent costs for protocol compatibility. The document emphasizes that native dual-stack connectivity is preferred when address space permits, but recognizes that translation and tunneling are now necessary tools.
sections.eli5: Engineers can solve these problems in different ways: by putting two address translators in a row, by splitting translation across two boxes, by sending old-style addresses through new-style networks in tunnels, or by translating between old and new styles.

sections.title: Operational and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The deployment of multiple NAT layers and translation mechanisms raises important considerations. Multiple layers of address translation can impact IPsec and other protocols that rely on transparent end-to-end addressing. Translation mechanisms may require modification of DNS responses, which has security implications documented in RFC 4966. Additionally, tunneling solutions introduce their own security questions around tunnel endpoint discovery and the risk of denial-of-service reflection attacks.

Network operations such as troubleshooting, logging, legal intercept, quality of service functions, and anti-spoofing measures all become more complex with multiple translation layers or translation between versions. Service providers deploying these scenarios must carefully document these operational consequences.
sections.eli5: When you translate addresses multiple times or tunnel packets, security tools like IPsec and DNS get confused. Network operators have to work harder to track traffic and prevent fraud.

sections.title: Standards Development and Next Steps
sections.content:
The RFC was originally written as input to a 2008 IETF interim meeting on co-existence, which led to the rechartering of the Behave and Softwire working groups to tackle these problems. By the time of publication in 2011, those groups had already begun developing standards: Softwire addressed the IPv4-over-IPv6 tunneling scenarios (including Dual-Stack Lite), and Behave addressed translation scenarios (including NAT64). The document serves as a historical record of the thinking that shaped these working groups and the rationale behind the standards they produced.

The RFC emphasizes that these new deployment models are complementary to, not replacements for, traditional dual-stack. Where sufficient address space exists, native dual-stack connectivity remains the most recommended approach.
sections.eli5: This note convinced the IETF to start working groups to build tools for these five problems. Those groups created standards that are still helping the internet work today.

left.title: Dual-Stack (Preferred)
left.desc: Host has both IPv4 and IPv6 connectivity; network has abundant address space.

right.title: Limited Address Space
right.desc: Hosts must share public addresses or reach servers via translation or tunneling.
